#249. RIIZE brought their online fandom into the real world. I was there to see it.

That was one of my first thoughts on Friday night as I watched K-pop group RIIZE perform for roughly 600 fans at Brooklyn Steel in New York City. There were no elaborate stage productions or arena-sized crowds. Instead, there were stripped-down performances, candid conversations, a few wonderfully awkward moments, and a sea of smartphones held high above the audience.

Seriously, everyone had their phones out.

It's a funny contradiction, considering the entire premise of the evening was to bring digital fandom into the physical world. But maybe that's just what being a fan looks like in 2026. Even when we're standing a few feet away from our favorite artists, we still want to capture the moment, preserve it, and inevitably share it with everyone who couldn't be there.

The occasion was Spotify CLOSER, a new live music series that brings artists and their most dedicated listeners together for intimate performances and conversations. After launching in Seoul in Oct., the series made its U.S. debut on Nov. 20 with RIIZE, bringing together more than 600 fans from the New York tri-state area, many of whom were identified as the group's top local listeners and selected based on their listening habits.

Since debuting under SM Entertainment in 2023, RIIZE — consisting of Shotaro, Eunseok, Sungchan, Wonbin, Sohee, and Anton — has emerged as one of K-pop's most prominent fifth-generation acts, performing at major festivals like Austin City Limits and Lollapalooza South America. But despite their growing international popularity, the group has only toured the U.S. once, making opportunities for American fans to see them in person relatively rare.

For many, their relationship with RIIZE has largely unfolded online, through music, livestreams, social media, and the seemingly endless stream of content that makes K-pop fandom feel like a full-time commitment.

In other words, the same platform that connected these fans to RIIZE's music was now bringing them face-to-face with the six people behind it. And I was curious to see what would happen when that connection moved offline.

Before RIIZE even took the stage, Spotify had transformed Brooklyn Steel into something of a playground for BRIIZE, the group's devoted fandom.

There was a fisheye photo station, branded Spotify x RIIZE microphone keychains, and an area where fans could write letters to the members. Nearby, six lockers offered a glimpse into each member's personality, decorated with objects representing their individual interests.

Shotaro's locker featured a camera and bucket hat, while Eunseok's included boxing gloves and a Doraemon plushie. Sungchan's was outfitted with a soccer ball and cleats, and Wonbin's displayed Nike Air Force 1s and earbuds. Sohee's locker featured a Boston cap and Naruto figures, while Anton's contained a violin and swimming goggles. Each member had also written a personal letter to BRIIZE.

For longtime fans, these weren't just random objects. They were familiar details, the kinds of things you pick up from watching livestreams and behind-the-scenes content. You can know an idol's favorite foods, recognize their sense of humor, and feel familiar with their friendships without ever having met them. Seeing these details arranged in physical space felt a little like stepping inside the digital world fans had spent years getting to know.

And that was the interesting thing about the event. Spotify wasn't simply bringing fans closer to RIIZE by putting them in a smaller room. It was recreating the familiarity of online fandom in a setting where fans could participate, leaving their own messages alongside the members' handwritten notes.

Of course, once RIIZE appeared, nearly every phone in the room went up, mine included. So much for going offline.

The crowd was enthusiastic and eager to interact, with handwritten signs scattered throughout the audience. My personal favorite was a sign directed at Anton that simply read, "Slap me." (I have questions, but I respect the commitment.)

Anton, who grew up in New Jersey, received particularly enthusiastic cheers from the Garden State contingent. There was also a very important geography lesson in which fans informed the members that Peter Parker, aka Spider-Man, is from New York. You know, the essential cultural exchange that happens when a K-pop group visits the city.

These were the kinds of interactions that made the evening feel less like a conventional concert and more like a gathering of people who already knew one another, even if most of them had never actually met.

And for RIIZE, it was an opportunity to put faces to the streaming numbers.

RIIZE opened the night with "Get A Guitar," their 2023 debut single, performed entirely in English for the first time. The setlist also included "Boom Boom Bass," "Impossible," "D-D-Done," "Love 119," and the first U.S. performance of "Do your dance."

But the evening wasn't just about the music. Between performances, the members participated in a Q&A hosted by Anton, who served as the group's unofficial emcee and occasional English translator. He kept the conversation moving, prompting his bandmates to answer questions and helping bridge the language gap with the predominantly English-speaking audience, while live subtitles appeared on the screens.

Initially, the members seemed a little reserved. Away from the familiar structure of a performance or the carefully edited chaos of variety content, there was a certain shyness to their early exchanges, as though they were still finding their footing in a more spontaneous setting.

But as the Q&A progressed, that initial hesitation gave way to something more playful. The members began teasing one another, laughing more freely, and engaging with the crowd. Sohee, in particular, seemed to come alive as the night went on. Funny, expressive, and naturally charismatic, he grew increasingly comfortable commanding the room, revealing a different side of the confidence he already brings to the stage as one of the group's standout vocalists.

It was fun to watch that transformation happen in real-time.

During one segment, the members voted on which of them best fit a series of superlatives. Sungchan was named the funniest, Anton earned the title of biggest flirt, and Shotaro received a unanimous vote for best smile. The conversations were sometimes silly, occasionally awkward, and all the more charming for it.

My favorite exchange came when Shotaro was expressing his appreciation for the fans. After delivering a heartfelt message, he earnestly added, "Please forget that."

Anton was quick to correct him: "Please don't forget that."

That small moment captured the easygoing charm of the night. RIIZE are a group accustomed to the precision of rehearsed performances, but here, in front of hundreds of fans, they were navigating something far less predictable. There was no choreography to fall back on, no script for a misplaced word or an unexpected laugh. Just six guys figuring it out together, and letting their personalities shine in the process.

For all the playful banter and fan interactions, the moment that stayed with me most was RIIZE's performance of their new single, "Insomnia."

The song is already one of the group's more understated offerings, performed without choreography, but for Spotify CLOSER, RIIZE took that intimacy a step further with a new, even more stripped-down arrangement. The performance put the focus squarely on their voices, allowing their harmonies to shine and giving the song a different kind of emotional weight. There was something lovely about hearing a song that was already relatively restrained given even more room to breathe.

It was the closest the evening came to the spirit of MTV Unplugged, the iconic music series that invited artists to reinterpret their work in a more intimate setting.

That's not to say RIIZE needed to abandon the choreography or elaborate performances that are so integral to K-pop. But there's something special about hearing artists approach their own material from a different perspective, especially when it brings out details that might otherwise go unnoticed.

Watching "Insomnia," I found myself missing that kind of music programming — the opportunity to see artists experiment with familiar songs, to hear their voices in a new context, and to experience a performance that feels entirely specific to a particular room and moment.

Spotify CLOSER isn't quite Unplugged, nor does it need to be. But the appeal feels similar. Sometimes, hearing a familiar song in a different way is enough to make you appreciate it all over again.

There's a certain irony in a streaming platform creating an event designed to bring fans away from their screens. Especially when nearly everyone in the room was holding up a phone.

Spotify CLOSER is, of course, a branded experience. It's a way to reward highly engaged listeners while creating exclusive content that can eventually circulate on the platform. Select performances from the evening will be released on Spotify, allowing fans around the world to experience some of what happened in Brooklyn.

But the commercial nature of the event doesn't make the connection any less meaningful. If anything, the night illustrated how intertwined our digital and physical experiences of fandom have become.

The fans at Brooklyn Steel didn't leave their online identities at the door. They brought their phones, their handwritten signs, their knowledge of the members' personalities, and all the inside jokes and shared references they'd accumulated from following RIIZE online. And the members, who initially seemed a little timid, gradually relaxed into the kind of playful, slightly clumsy interactions fans have come to love through their screens.

As the evening drew to a close, RIIZE expressed their hopes of returning to New York before ending with an encore performance of "One Kiss."

For all the ways technology has made artists more accessible than ever, there's still something it can't quite replicate: the spontaneity of sharing a room, where a mistranslated word can become a joke, a fan's sign can spark a conversation, and a familiar song can sound entirely new.

And for the record, Shotaro, I won't forget that.

Crystal Bell is the Digital Culture Editor at Mashable, where she leads coverage of the creator economy, internet culture, and digital life. She also oversees the Mashable 101, the publication's annual list recognizing the internet's most influential creators.

She's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in New York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

#248. How to Win Big Betting on Jensen Huang? Listen to Trump

Just days ago, Jensen Huang’s chances of returning as Nvidia CEO looked increasingly slim, at least according to prediction markets. Earlier this month, Huang resigned from the AI hardware giant following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence services. As more reports emerged about Huang’s alleged bad behavior, Nvidia’s board insisted it had no plans to reinstate him. By early Sunday morning on the East Coast, traders on Polymarket’s US platform put his chances of returning at just 10 percent. But by Monday, Huang was back in charge.

The swings in Huang’s odds on prediction markets offer a window into how his unlikely comeback unfolded and who saw it coming. The New York Times reported that President Trump played a crucial role in convincing the board to bring Huang back. Traders who paid attention to what Trump and his allies wanted appear to have fared much better than those who did not.

On Sunday evening in Washington, Huang’s odds on Polymarket US jumped six percentage points in just 40 minutes after Trump published a Truth Social missive calling for Huang’s reinstatement. The president said he wanted to help revive the stock market, which had plunged following Huang’s scandal, a sign of Nvidia’s enormous influence over the AI industry and broader US economy.

According to the prediction market intelligence firm Betting Intelligence, odds on both Kalshi and Polymarket’s markets largely tracked with public signals about the likelihood of Huang’s return. They rose when Huang said he was open to returning, fell when the board dismissed the possibility, and climbed again when President Trump threw his support behind the former CEO. But there were several large trades that could not be tied to public developments.

Betting Intelligence and the prediction market forensics firm MSR Decode identified clusters of trades on Huang’s return that did not appear to be driven by news or public commentary. Kalshi and Polymarket declined to comment on whether they are currently investigating potential insider trading in markets related to Huang’s return.

Despite these anomalies, Betting Intelligence CEO Dan Zimmermann says the Huang-related markets showed fewer signs of potentially suspicious activity than usual. “The group that could have known the board’s decision in advance was small. So the market was mostly headline chasers and longshot buyers,” he says.

For traders who profited from Huang’s comeback, the lesson is clear: Don’t discount Trump.

Isaac Rose-Berman, a research and policy fellow at the American Institute for Boys & Men and professional sports bettor, says he made approximately $10,000 wagering on Huang’s return on Kalshi. He placed his trade after the Nvidia chief said on X that he was open to reclaiming his old job. Rose-Berman says that he figured that the board would consider Huang’s return if it looked likely to improve the company’s stock performance. (Never mind the concerns about national security or Huang allegedly threatening employees that he would “pee in your brain.”) “It’s 2026 and Trump is president, scandal schmandal,” Rose-Berman says. “Should’ve bet more.”

A pseudonymous prediction market trader known as Domer tells WIRED he cleared approximately $600,000 by placing an early wager last week on Huang’s return. He wasn’t focused explicitly on Trump’s desires, but he says his understanding of power dynamics ultimately guided his approach. “Boards can be very malleable,” he tells WIRED.

Other prediction market “sharps” say that commentary from Trumpworld was the strongest signal available about Huang’s return. As some bettors noted, there was a notable opportunity for profit after Trump suggested to a PBS NewsHour reporter that Huang would be back in power soon, but before Nvidia officially announced his reinstatement. “The key was looking at Trump’s support and the recent performance of the stock market,” says Kalshi trader Caleb Davies.

Aaron Courtney, a data analyst and cofounder of a prediction market analytics firm, says he took a loss on his Huang position. Looking back, he says his mistake was not paying attention to what Trump and other administration officials said over the weekend. “Trump saying he hoped Nvidia would bring Jensen back would be the clearest signal,” he says.

#247. Nvidias board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO following Trumps endorsement

Updated on Monday, Nov. 23 at 12:45 p.m. ET — This story has been updated with additional information on how Wall Street is responding to Jensen Huang's return and additional details on why the board reversed course.

The Nvidia board of directors has voted unanimously to reinstate the embattled Jensen Huang as the company's CEO, the board announced in a surprise statement Monday morning. The move follows President Donald Trump publicly calling for Huang's return as CEO.

Huang famously resigned on Nov. 12 following reports from the New York Times and the Financial Times that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. In the days that followed, revelations of two more alleged extramarital affairs — with Nvidia employees, no less — emerged, seemingly sealing the CEO's fate.

On Nov. 12, Huang announced he was resigning his position as CEO, a role he'd held since he co-founded the company in 1993. Under his leadership, Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world, and in recent years, Nvidia chips have powered the fast-growing AI industry.

In reinstating Huang, the board cited "input from senior levels of the United States government...that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk."

President Trump called the board's surprise decision "correct and proper" in a post on his Truth Social website. #246. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#245. Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider on Monday vowed that Germany will continue to move away from burning fossil fuels despite the failure of the COP31 declaration in Antalya, Turkey, this weekend.

Speaking at an event in Potsdam, Schneider said: "We will clearly maintain our course on climate protection in Europe and Germany, but above all one that makes us independent of oil and gas because otherwise we are vulnerable to blackmail and our economic performance becomes extremely volatile."

Schneider expressed disappointment less at the result of the two-week conference than its format, which he said was far more focussed on spectacle than substance.

Speaking of his vision for a format for future climate conferences, Schneider said: "Basically, I don't need so many people there. What I need are the relevant decision makers with whom I negotiate and make decisions."

Although he voiced relief that the final document from the conference had not represented a step backwards — as well as stressing that some 30 countries had pledged to maintain the move away from fossil fuels — Schneider acknowledged that it had been nearly impossible to find consensus with Russia and Saudi Arabia at the table.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius urged calm over reports that Russia was planning to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space as early as next month.

"First of ​all, ‌let's remain calm, because there are reports — that's true — but ‌it's ​not clear what kind of weapons these are, and the ​effect they might have depends, in ⁠turn, ​on where they ​are deployed," Pistorius told ​reporters in ‌Berlin.

"Therefore, it's too early to ​speculate ⁠publicly about this. We are consulting ⁠internally ​and taking the necessary measures."

German public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung first reported on the matter, which said that internal intelligence reports circulated among NATO countries earlier this month said that Russia was ready to bring the alleged satellite, named Sputnik-S, out of storage in Moscow.

The reports said Russia may be planning to launch it as soon as December.

Nuclear weapons are banned in orbit by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, of which Moscow is a signatory.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said not allowing Ukraine intoNATO in 2008 was a mistake.

At the2008 summit in Bucharest, Romania, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy argued that they weren't ready to extend NATO membership to Ukraine.

US President George W. Bush said he was in favor of having Ukraine enter into NATO.

But both Germany and France said that that would hurt relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The NATO summit then decided that Ukraine would eventually join the alliance, but offered no timetable.

At a press conference on Monday, Merz was asked about whether he thinks the time was right to talk about Ukraine's membership in NATO.

To which Merz said, "If it [Ukraine] had become a member of NATO, this war could probably have been prevented."

Merz meant Russia's war against Ukraine when he said "this war" at the press conference after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Angela Merkel defended her decision at the Bucharest summit as of 2024 as well, saying a large proportion of the Ukrainian population had opposed joining NATO at the time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.

Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.

"Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz said.

Merz said Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.

German startup investments in fields such as robotics and defense are set to almost triple this year, a study noted on Monday.

The German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation study predicted that investments in so-called "deep tech startups" will surge from just €2.9 billion ($3.17 billion) last year to 8.1 billion ($8.9 billion) this year.

The study described the rise as a "major success for Germany as a business location."

"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

The study also showed about 300 new deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.

Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.

The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools."

Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a new chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.

The party announced on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.

Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.

The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

There are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder. The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.

A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.

Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW  were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.

The strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it says was circulated at the start of November.

It said that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report said the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin said the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

German exports to Africa have reached a new record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.

Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

The biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.

The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention plans to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

Police are investigating a suspected case of aggravated arson after a fire broke out at a hospital in Berlin.

Investigators believe a patient set fire to his bed in a room on the first floor of one of the hospital buildings in the Lichtenberg district on Sunday evening.

One nurse and the suspected arsonist suffered smoke inhalation and had to be treated in hospital. Overall, 15 people were injured with another 13 suffering from minor injuries.

While firefighters managed to put out the flames, smoke spread to other parts of the hospital which then had to be evacuated.

#242. Google rolls out new search homepage with AI chat history and no search button

Google search is making it even easier to access AI tools on the search page.

Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that has been in testing for the past few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image-generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that sat next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

The other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged in to Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”

It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

This change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

#240. What is Sound Glow on HomePods, and how do you get it on your Apple speaker?

Apple’s latest HomePod update makes the top of your speaker glow in sync with music.

Apple's HomePod has a basic set of lights on top that don't do much beyond glowing when Siri is listening or when something is playing. But following the launch of the HomePod mini 2, Apple also introduced a new feature called Sound Glow that makes better use of these lights. When turned on, the top of the speaker becomes a colorful light show synced to the song you're listening to — and the good news is that it's not exclusive to the latest HomePod mini. The feature is part of HomePod Software 27.2 and also works with the original HomePod mini and the HomePod 2 (the larger model). Here's a breakdown of how Sound Glow works and how you can enable (or disable) it on your HomePods.

HomePods don't have a traditional display like Apple's HomeView. Instead, Apple has included an array of LEDs on top along with a touch-sensitive surface that lets users access quick controls such as volume and play/pause. With the latest HomePod software update, these LEDs are now used to make HomePods a little more fun with Sound Glow. Now, when you play a song, the speaker pulls colors from the album art and pulses them in time with the music's beat. Listening to Taylor Swift's The Life of a Showgirl will result in predominantly green and orange lights, while Miley Cyrus's Endless Summer Vacation will make the lights on your HomePod turn blue.

Apple says that the light animation reacts in real time to the bass and treble of the song being played, so two songs from the same album will glow differently. Also, Sound Glow isn't limited to songs — it also works with podcasts and Apple's ambient sounds. For instance, the Rain soundscape features an animation with a gentle pitter-patter effect. Songs without artwork or videos revert to the HomePod's standard white light. It all happens automatically and you really don't have to think about it.

There are a few limitations worth noting, though. Don't expect Sound Glow to fully light up your living room — the lights aren't bright enough to do that unless the room is completely dark. The feature is also not available on the original HomePod released in 2018, even though it can be updated to the latest HomePod software. You'll also need an Apple Intelligence-enabled device paired with your HomePods for Sound Glow to work — that means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, an M1 Mac or newer or one of the latest iPads. An Apple TV running tvOS 27 also does the trick to enable Sound Glow on your HomePods.

If you have HomePods and a compatible Apple device, setting up Sound Glow is easy, but you'll need to make sure they're all running the latest software first. That means HomePod Software 27.2 or later on your HomePods and iOS 27.2 on your iPhone or iPad. HomePods usually update automatically after a while, but you can confirm in the Home app from another Apple device. Tap the three-dot button and select Home Settings, then look for the Software Update menu. Even a brand-new HomePod mini 2 may need a software update, since it may ship with a version prior to 27.2 installed.

Once everything is up to date, you can finally enable Sound Glow. Go back to the Home app's main screen and tap your HomePod, then go to Settings and scroll down until you find the Sound Glow toggle. Just flip it on, and the feature will work — you'll need to do this for each HomePod individually. Ask Siri to play a song or use AirPlay on your iPhone to try out Sound Glow and see if it's working. And if you don't like Sound Glow, turning it off requires pretty much the same steps as turning it on, but now you'll have to flip the toggle to off instead.

#239. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#238. SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

“Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026.”

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

“SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has said that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

“My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”

The communications from Himes suggest that congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

“It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

Various options are open to congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

It seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or launches, as the company is currently providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

#236. Michelle Branchs Are You Happy Now? is having a TikTok renaissance thanks to Netflixs The Body

Michelle Branch has a question for Gen Z: Are you happy now?

More than two decades after its release, the singer-songwriter's 2003 breakup anthem "Are You Happy Now?" is finding a new audience on TikTok, thanks to a particularly memorable needle drop in Netflix's buzzy teen horror drama The Body. And for millennials who grew up screaming along to the song in their bedrooms, the sudden resurgence feels like a long-overdue moment of recognition — and another painful reminder that we're all old AF.

Welcome to the Michelle Branch renaissance. We've been expecting you.

The song appears in the third episode of The Body, a psychological horror series set at a Catholic girls' school in 2004, where a dance team initiation spirals into a supernatural panic. The show's early-aughts setting provides plenty of opportunities for nostalgic needle drops, with a soundtrack featuring Kelly Clarkson, Ciara, Kylie Minogue, and No Doubt. But Branch's angsty pop-rock hit gets one of the show's most memorable musical moments.

During a church service, Elise puts on a convincing display of demonic possession, collapsing as the song builds toward its explosive chorus. The juxtaposition of religious imagery, teenage hysteria, and Branch's soaring vocals makes for a scene practically engineered to go viral.

And that's exactly what's happening on social media.

Originally released in 2003 as the lead single from Branch's supremely underrated sophomore album, Hotel Paper, "Are You Happy Now?" became one of the defining songs of the early-2000s pop-rock boom. With its crunchy guitars, emotionally charged vocals, and deliciously confrontational chorus, the track captured a particular kind of teenage heartbreak — the kind that demands to be felt at full volume.

It was a time when young women like Branch, Avril Lavigne, and Vanessa Carlton were helping shape the sound of mainstream pop, bringing guitars, messy emotions, and confessional songwriting to a generation of listeners. They embraced teenage melodrama, not shied away from it.

Now, more than 20 years later, that sound is resonating with a new generation. Just look at the comments on the song's YouTube music video, where the top comment asks, "Who's here after The Body?"

On TikTok, younger listeners are discovering the cathartic power of Branch's early-aughts angst. One user declared it the new background song to their life, while another thanked The Body for introducing them to this "cunty asf song." Others are already looking to expand their musical horizons. "I've been obsessed with this song since The Body," one user wrote, asking for recommendations for artists with a similar sound.

But the nostalgia goes beyond the music itself. One TikToker lamented being born in 2004 instead of getting to experience the year as a teenager, adding, "God I'm SO jealous of millennials." Another praised the show's music supervisor with a particularly heartfelt blessing: "Whoever put this soundtrack together, I hope both sides of your pillow are cold cause wow, you get it."

The resurgence is part of a familiar pattern in which television and social media introduce younger audiences to older music. Kate Bush's "Running Up That Hill" famously experienced a massive revival after appearing in Stranger Things, while TikTok has repeatedly turned decades-old tracks into contemporary hits.

What makes "Are You Happy Now?" particularly well-suited to this moment is that its emotional intensity never really went out of style. The song's combination of wounded pride, anger, and catharsis translates just as easily to a TikTok edit as it did to a burned CD in 2003.

For Gen Z, it might be a new discovery. For millennials, it's confirmation of something we've known all along: Michelle Branch was always that girl.

For a generation that grew up online, the early 2000s have become something of a cultural fantasy. From Y2K fashion and digital cameras to wired headphones and the resurgence of pop-rock, Gen Z has embraced the aesthetics of a time when the internet still seemed full of possibility. More recently, the "millennial optimism" trend has romanticized the late 2000s and early 2010s, when Tumblr aesthetics, twee fashion, and earnest indie music dominated the internet. It's quite the turnaround for a generation that once made mocking millennial cringe something of a pastime.

But millennial optimism is about more than nostalgia for a particular aesthetic. It's a longing for a time when the future seemed brighter, when hope and sincerity felt less embarrassing, and when pop culture wasn't quite so steeped in irony. Of course, the past wasn't nearly as carefree as nostalgia might suggest. Still, there's something appealing about the emotional earnestness of that era, especially its music.

And while "Are You Happy Now?" might not exactly embody millennial optimism, its resurgence taps into that same longing for a seemingly simpler cultural moment. The platforms might have changed how we discover music, but the desire to scream along to a song that understands exactly how you feel hasn't changed much at all.

Next up: Justice for Carlton's "White Houses."

#234. Is Spotify still tracking your listening for Wrapped 2026? Heres what we know.

Every year, as Spotify Wrapped season approaches, a familiar kind of panic sets in. You start mentally calculating how many times you've streamed your favorite artist, wondering whether that one song you played obsessively in Feb. will come back to haunt you, and perhaps making a last-minute attempt to influence your results.

Recently, someone asked me who I thought my top artist would be this year, and for the first time in a long time, I genuinely had no idea. Stray Kids have held that spot for the past four years, but with fewer new releases from the group in 2026, my listening habits have been a little more unpredictable. I've spent the year bouncing between artists and genres, which means my top five could be anyone's guess. (And yes, I'm a little nervous about that.)

After all, Spotify Wrapped isn't just a recap of what you listened to. It's become a public declaration of your musical identity, one that inevitably ends up on Instagram Stories for everyone to judge.

But with Nov. nearly over and Spotify Wrapped 2026 expected to arrive in early Dec., there's one important question: Is Spotify still tracking your listening habits?

Spotify has not confirmed the exact cutoff date for Wrapped 2026. However, based on how the company has handled previous editions, your listening data likely stopped counting sometime in mid-Nov.

For years, a persistent rumor suggested that Spotify stopped collecting data for Wrapped on Oct. 31, leaving the final two months of the year out of your annual recap. But that's not quite how it works.

In 2025, Spotify confirmed that Wrapped included listening activity from Jan. 1 through mid-Nov., just a few weeks before its Dec. 3 release. The company explained that it needs time to process listening data and prepare millions of personalized recaps ahead of launch.

So while Spotify continues recording your listening activity for its regular features and recommendations, that doesn't necessarily mean your late-Nov. streams will count toward Wrapped 2026.

Until Spotify confirms this year's tracking window, there's no way to know for certain.

If you're hoping to push a particular artist into your top five before Wrapped arrives, you may already be out of luck.

Even if Spotify is still counting streams, a few days of obsessive listening probably won't dramatically change the habits you've accumulated over the past 11 months.

But there's an important distinction between how Spotify calculates your top songs and top artists. According to Spotify's explanation of its Wrapped methodology, your top songs are ranked by the number of times you've listened to them, with each play counting after more than 30 seconds. Your top artists, meanwhile, are determined using a weighted stream count that gives primary artists more credit than featured performers.

That means an artist whose entire discography you've been listening to all year could rank higher than someone responsible for your single most-played song.

In other words, your Wrapped results aren't necessarily as straightforward as counting how many times you've played your favorite track.

Maybe you're less concerned about getting your favorite artist to No. 1 and more worried about the songs you don't want showing up in your results. Fortunately, Spotify gives users some control over what influences their Wrapped.

In a Nov. 5 announcement, Spotify reminded listeners that they can exclude individual tracks and playlists from their Taste Profile, preventing those streams from influencing certain Wrapped results and everyday recommendations.

Open Spotify and find the track or playlist.

Select "Exclude from your taste profile." (You can reverse the decision by selecting "Include in your taste profile.")

Spotify says this setting applies to past and future listening, meaning you can remove a particularly embarrassing musical obsession from your taste-based results even after you've spent hours streaming it.

There's also a dedicated setting for kids' and family music, which is especially useful for parents who don't want their children's favorite songs dominating their year-end recap.

One caveat: Excluded listening can still contribute to your total minutes listened. It just won't shape your taste-based rankings.

Spotify hasn't announced an official release date, but Wrapped typically arrives in late Nov. or early Dec.

Last year's edition launched on Dec. 3, while the 2024 and 2023 editions arrived on Dec. 4 and Nov. 29, respectively. If Spotify follows its recent pattern of Wednesday releases, Dec. 2, 2026, is a possibility, though the company has yet to confirm that date.

Until then, you can keep listening to whatever you want. Whether those streams make it into your Wrapped is another question entirely.

And perhaps that's for the best. The fun of Spotify Wrapped has always been discovering what your listening habits reveal about you, even when the results aren't quite what you expected.

#233. Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says that its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”

Gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

#232. What the green flashing light on your Roku remote is telling you

A remote that won't cooperate can put your streaming plans on hold. Here's how to work out what's wrong and get back to the content you love.

Regardless of what you think of Fox's takeover, Roku is still an undeniable force in smart TVs. The company's products are an easy choice when looking for the best streaming devices, and of course a number of TVs now ship with Roku OS built in, most notably models from TCL and Hisense. Roku is the main game in town for brands that are not using Google TV, Fire TV or their own proprietary software.

One of the reasons for the platform's popularity is its simplicity. That said, there are times when the platform can be a little obtuse, mysterious blinking lights on the remote being a prime example. It's easy to assume that means a problem — but what, exactly?

If you're dealing with a flashing green LED on your Roku remote, the fix could be very straightforward, simply requiring fresh batteries or a recharge, depending on the model. In some circumstances, however, you may need to do more or replace your remote entirely. Hopefully you've already got the Roku app on your phone as a backup, which can save you in a pinch when your remote is on the fritz.

As we just suggested, one reason for the light may be that your remote's batteries are low. If that's the case, swapping in new batteries (if there's no built-in one) should quickly solve the problem. If you find this is happening too frequently, though, it may be because you're using rechargeable batteries. Alkalines are costlier in the long run — but Roku does recommend them for remotes with replaceable batteries. You can check battery levels in advance by navigating to Settings > Remotes & devices > Remotes > Your remote > About.

You'll also see this light if you're trying to set up a replacement remote. Using your old one or the Roku app, you may need to head to Settings > Remotes & devices > Add devices > Remote > Continue to complete the process. You'll definitely see green flashing if you trigger a remote's physical pairing controls, which is done by holding a dedicated button or the Back and Home buttons simultaneously for five seconds.

There's no need to be worried unless the light is flashing rapidly after re-pairing. If that's going on, it's a sign that your remote is probably broken and needs to be replaced. Note that you can also buy third-party remotes; sticking with one of Roku's official options should get you better support and features. Whatever you choose, verify that it's going to be compatible with your particular TV or streamer.

If you've run through all of the above steps short of replacing your remote, one remaining option is to restart it. If it uses replaceable batteries, take them out, then press any two buttons before reinserting the batteries, negative sides first. If it uses a built-in battery, hold down its physical pairing controls (see the last section) for 20 seconds.

At this point, there's not much else you can try short of clearing the cache on your Roku or updating or rebooting your Roku device, or you could learn how to reset your Roku. Be warned that if you try a reset, you'll have to reconfigure everything as if it were right out of the box. It's also unlikely to solve a green light issue, since as we've established, that's normally related to battery levels or pairing, not buggy software.

If worst comes to worst, you may be stuck using your phone for control. One pro tip, though — you don't always have to use the Roku app. If your setup supports AirPlay from iPhone or MacBook to your TV or screen mirroring on Roku with your Android phone, you can often cut to the chase with whatever audio or video it is you're trying to play.

#230. The pros and cons of wearing your Fitbit around your ankle

An ankle-worn Fitbit can catch steps your wrist misses, though some health metrics may suffer.

It's frustrating when you've finished your daily walk, but Fitbit didn't catch all the steps because it couldn't recognize them. Or when you've pushed a stroller, held the treadmill rails or worked at a walking desk, and discovered that limited arm movement makes your brisk walk look unimpressive in the app. Out of all the Fitbit hacks, tricks and tips out there, this basic problem has persisted for many users.

Some have found a way around this by wearing their Fitbit on their ankle. It may seem like a strange fix, but having the motion sensor closer to your feet can help. Fitbit devices measure more than just steps, but they depend on arm movement to gather data. While Google often assumes you're wearing the Fitbit on your wrist, activities with limited arm movement mean your health data may not be accurate.

Fitbit trackers use accelerometers to recognize movement patterns associated with walking, but a wrist-worn sensor can miss steps when your arms remain still. Google acknowledges that pushing a stroller or shopping cart can lead to missed steps. Walking pads create similar issues when you're typing at your desk rather than allowing your arms to swing. In these cases, an ankle-worn Fitbit measures leg movement directly. It also keeps your wrist free if you dislike wearing watches or if your workplace bans wrist-wear.

There's some evidence behind the idea. In a 2025 study, 11 healthy adults walked with a single-point cane or two-wheeled walker while wearing Fitbit Inspire 3 trackers on their wrists, hips and ankles. The hip and ankle placements had a combined average step-count error of 1.5 percent, while wrist readings were substantially less reliable. It's a significant difference, but keep in mind this small study involved assisted walking, not daily activities.

The concept isn't all that novel, either. The Moov Now supported ankle wear back in 2015 and was specifically designed for it, unlike current Fitbits.

Wearing a Fitbit on your ankle doesn't automatically translate to what you're doing. In a test, a Fitbit Versa 4 logged 1,510 steps during a 30-minute stationary bike session when worn on the ankle, versus 180 when the same tracker was worn on the wrist. Pedaling an exercise bike isn't the same as steps, and you're likely more interested in monitoring heart-rate. Also, the tracker did fail to record sleep during a nighttime ankle test.

Speaking of heart-rate, Fitbit's optical sensors measure blood-volume changes through the skin to estimate your pulse, and Google recommends wearing the device snugly against your wrist. The company hasn't established comparable accuracy for ankle placement, where fit and sensor contact differ.

A recent experiment summed up the debate. The ankle-worn Fitbit Air picked up walking pad steps the wrist-worn Pixel Watch 4 missed while the reviewer was typing. Conversely, one walk produced a heart-rate peak of 182 beats per minute on the ankle-worn Fitbit, compared to 129 bpm maximum measured on the wrist. Four more walks failed to repeat the spike, so it's not conclusive proof ankle readings are always incorrect.

Finally, Fitbit looks fine on the ankle, but standard wristbands may be too short. Aftermarket ankle straps cost extra and a loose tracker can rub uncomfortably against socks or shoes. And of course, checking notifications is difficult. For those who want to keep their wrist free, the Fitbit Inspire 3 also has an official clothing clip option, but this mode does not include heart-rate tracking, Active Zone Minutes or automatic exercise tracking.
