The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.

Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric.

“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this”

To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.

“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit.

Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice).

With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever.

To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside.

Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency.

“That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event.

In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found.

To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation.

Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall.

“Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”

“In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”

There was some progress. Around 80 nations signed onto a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy consumption to 35 percent over the next decade, according to COP31 president Murat Kurum. The list of countries that includes, however, hasn’t been published yet, Carbon Brief reports.

Another voluntary pledge to keep AI from derailing climate action by calling on data centers to run on less polluting energy also failed to garner much support. Douglas notes that by using the term “low-emission energy,” the pledge still leaves the door open for natural gas (which produces less carbon pollution than coal when burned but is a significant source of methane pollution) to keep powering data centers.

“The Antalya A.I. pledge is a step in the right direction to address an important piece of the impacts, but needs teeth in order to translate into stronger protections for people and the planet,” the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council said in a statement when the pledge was first announced. “The speed, scale and scope of this challenge is bigger than perhaps anything before it, and the guardrails must be commensurate.”

#170. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#168. States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

X says every Grok output is screened, but state AGs say Grok is still making CSAM.

On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.

“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”

Millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.

“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said in a press release.

States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.

Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”

“Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.

Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the company has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety said that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.

“When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”

However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises users how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.

Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok users, states alleged.

Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”

In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”

“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”

It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”

As NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.

“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.

Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to users.

“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.

Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of users Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.

“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones said. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”

If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $299 ($100 off) at Amazon and Walmart, beating its most sale price by $30. If you prefer a larger size, the 46mm model is on sale for $349 ($100 off) at Amazon and Walmart, beating its previous low by $30.

The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around.

It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day.

I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened.

Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now.

The deal was reportedly brokered by Peter Thiel’s very own boy

I have argued here, in the past, that the Epstein case laid bare the real politics of the revanchist American right wing: total elite impunity. Well, here it is again! If you are close enough with Trump, it doesn’t matter if you may have jeopardized national security by fucking an alleged Chinese spy. You won’t even be investigated for it before the American president calls in to your board of directors’ meeting to demand you be reinstated. I mean, it is the era of gangster tech regulation — what were any of us expecting? The deal was reportedly brokered by Peter Thiel’s very own boy, Vance.

Just so we can be absolutely clear about what transpired at Nvidia, let’s quickly go through the facts as we know them. A Chinese citizen named Alice Huang acquired the company she renamed Megaspeed, the Singaporean data firm at the center of this inquiry, in 2023. At some point, Huang met Huang, and the two were seen together at a dinner that December. From 2024 to 2025, Megaspeed received more than 200 Nvidia shipments.

In September 2025, the US government began investigating Megaspeed for possible violations of chip export controls; that October, the State Department told Trump of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, who was described as a Chinese intelligence asset. Also in October, The New York Times first reported on Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia. In December, Trump — who has a close relationship with Jensen Huang — allowed Nvidia to sell more powerful chips to China. In March 2026, Marco Rubio warned the government about Alice, and Trump nonetheless invited Huang to a visit in China. In October, The New York Times reported on the affair. Shortly after Huang sent a note to Nvidia admitting to it, several other reports of infidelity — this time with Nvidia employees — surfaced. On November 12th, Huang resigned. On November 17th, during the Nvidia earnings call, the board’s chair said that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On November 23rd, Huang was back.

This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive

What changed between last week and this week? A week was not enough time to truly review all the information on Huang and his paramour, Alice “No Relation” Huang, the international woman of mystery. The explanation seems to be that Nvidia’s board succumbed to a pressure campaign from Huang’s fellow billionaires, and a direct intervention from the president and vice president of the United States of America.

Sure, all these CEOs ostensibly wanted Huang back at Nvidia to keep the AI trade going. Still, watching the likes of Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick, investing loudmouth Bill Ackman, and Elon Musk — who actually did appear in the Epstein files, and who seemed to be pretty friendly with Epstein! — pitch a fit last week was instructive. These men worried that they might be punished for wrongdoing, that they did not get big enough to be above the law. They have now been reassured, and I suppose that is what really matters. After all, Trump said on CNBC that he gave Nvidia’s board assurances that Jensen is “absolutely fine.”

This level of open corruption is genuinely impressive, and not just because Huang is CEO of Nvidia again. Almost in passing, Trump noted that he had “protected” Musk in his first term from “a certain incident [that] took place, a very tough incident.” In his own inimitable style, Trump told Jim Cramer, “You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally.

Surely there is no possible downside when the CEOs of two of the biggest corporations on Earth owe their jobs to Trump personally

One thing that has perhaps emboldened this crew is the stance from professional politics-knowers — and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries — that holding members of the Trump administration accountable might be a hindrance to governing. That accountability was part of the reason for the blue wave in November seems to have bypassed these pundits (and the presumptive House majority leader). But then, why should we believe that Democrats will thoroughly investigate this? Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is claiming to want an investigation, but I am skeptical of how deep that investigation will go as long as Schumer leads it, and only partially because he’s been allied with Silicon Valley for more than a decade. He also has a daughter who works at OpenAI, a company that Nvidia invests in and that is dependent on Nvidia chips. How hard is he really willing to go?

Of course, there may be more to this than just pure economic self-interest. In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump posted a remarkable image. It is an altered picture of Trump himself, taken after a failed assassination attempt in 2024. Trump’s head has been replaced with Jensen Huang’s head. The American flag has been replaced with the Nvidia logo. Huang is waving a bright red bra. It seems I owe Sigmund Freud an apology. In the end, these men fear nothing more than losing power for sexual shenanigans — and especially losing power to a woman.

Leave aside the national security issues for a minute and focus on the two Nvidia employees. Dating subordinates is a serious conflict of interest; the CEO of Nestle lost his job for just that last year. This is a major violation for CEOs of normal companies, but it is common practice among the sleazeballs of Silicon Valley: Bill Gates is famous for it and it was plainly rampant at Google, a tone set by Sergey Brin himself. I am sure that you will be shocked, shocked to discover that in the wake of MeToo, Brin was among the men who suddenly swung right. I mean, Musk himself announced he was a Republican the day before Business Insider reported that he exposed himself to a flight attendant and paid hush money to cover it up.

If you’re rich enough, and connected enough, everything is permitted

The Republican Party has made the abuse of women without consequences one of its main issues; that the lesser violation of sleeping with subordinates would also be something the revanchists would defend seems obvious. That was clear from the botched investigation of the Epstein affair itself, the botched release of the Epstein files, and the assorted confirmation hearings of Pete Hegseth, Brett Kavanaugh, and Todd Blanche. (To say nothing of the Andrew Tate business.) But in all this, let’s not forget that Trump has been accused of sexual misconduct by no fewer than 28 women. So I’m sure it was an affront to all these guys that not only did Huang’s misconduct include a series of affairs, but he was also replaced by Colette Kress, who is known to be a woman.

I suppose we might as well pass by the various reports that Huang allegedly terrorized his employees. In light of everything else, this seems minor by comparison.

Anyway I had that all in mind when I saw Epic’s Sweeney celebrating the state intrusion into theoretically private companies by posting “Back in Black,” an oblique reference to Huang’s leather jackets that is also from the later, lesser period of AC/DC, after Bon Scott died and AC/DC became an AC/DC tribute band. He also called The New York Times’ reporting into Huang “lies.” Musk continued his streak of Sephiroth posting: “The mistake has been corrected.” Jason Calacanis, the All-In podcast’s village idiot, posted, “GPU Jesus has risen!” along with an openly blasphemous, AI-generated image of Huang as Christ.

Best of luck to Joon Kim, the Wachtell Lipton partner and former federal prosecutor who is conducting “a thorough and independent investigation” into Huang’s alleged misconduct on behalf of Nvidia’s board. I assume Kim has, like the rest of us, gotten the message loud and clear: If you’re rich enough, and connected enough, everything is permitted. Or perhaps, more succinctly: lol nothing matters.

#164. COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy

COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?

The longest-running climate talks in history came to a disappointing conclusion on Sunday as negotiators failed to come to an agreement on a shared political direction on climate change.

After two days of extended talks, representatives from country after country, tiredness etched into each face, voiced their opposition to the so-called "Antalya Pact."

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," said Murat Kurum, Turkish president of the COP31 climate summit.

One of the main sticking points: the words "fossil fuels." While some nations, including petrostates like Saudi Arabia and Russia, wanted them omitted from the text, others saw it as a "step backwards" not to include them.

Around 130 parties — among them vulnerable island nations, developing countries and richer EU members — called for the reintroduction of the two words into the text, to no avail. And so many refused to support the adoption of the final COP agreement.

The deadlock signals a failure for the UN process. But the number of countries willing to walk away from what they saw as a weak text was, arguably, a show of strength, and one that had been long coming.

The phrase "fossil fuels" first appeared three years ago in the closing decision of COP28 in Dubai with the promise of "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems, in just, orderly and equitable manner." But it has been omitted from every text since.

Yet this year's climate summit was the first to acknowledge that the world will breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that scientists said would safeguard the world from the worst impacts of planetary heating.

And so, the pressure was on for progress; to turn pledges from previous years into concrete action. But that progress didn't come.

"We don't celebrate the deep divisions exposed or the lack of a political signal from COP31 capable of driving climate action in line with science, equity and the law," said Nikki Reisch, director of the climate and energy program at the Center for International Environmental Law.

"But the rejected text would have done more harm than good."

The lack of agreement was not solely about fossil fuels; money also played a part.

Developing nations have long argued that they need additional financing, both as a means for them to move away from coal, oil and gas, but also to help them cope with the consequences of rising temperatures.

Countries all over the world are being battered by extreme weather events. Catastrophes like flooding, drought and wildfires have been fueled and worsened by rising global temperatures. Often the worst hit are poorer countries with low rates of greenhouse gas emissions.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And yet, richer states behind much of the historical emissions are increasingly unwilling to foot the bill. Dissatisfaction at home due to higher food and fuel prices has left many governments loathe to pay more to finance climate action abroad.

With the United States  — the world's biggest historical emitter  — now absent from negotiations and on the verge of leaving the United Nation's Framework Convention on Climate Change, the European Union was portrayed as this year's villain with some observers accusing the EU of hypocrisy.

"You can't demand action and then block the finance that makes this possible," Fanny Petitbon, policy analyst at 350.org, said in a statement.

As the world's largest provider of climate finance, the EU reportedly refused to negotiate on providing additional finance and has repeatedly called for other nations to step up.

The failure to find an agreement is a particularly bitter turn of events for countries that face ever worsening impacts of climate change, like the island states that are being confronted by a reality that could see their countries wiped off the map as sea levels rise.

Although the Turkey-led electrification agenda calling for an increase in global electricity consumption to 35% by 2035 was not formally adopted — it made up part of the rejected final agreement — more than 90 countries pledged to move forward regardless.

It's not a silver bullet. There was no agreement on ensuring the increase was forged only through clean, renewable energy. But it would still signal forward momentum, driven by economic forces and a need for home-grown energy security.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And there are other hopes. The second conference on the Just Transition Away from Fossil Fuels will take place in Tuvalu in July 2027. Initiated at the COP30 conference last year in Belem, Brazil, it has seen increasing support from countries putting together concrete roadmaps for abandoning coal, oil and gas.

There has been much talk of blame and who is responsible for the breakdown and collapse of talks. What is clear is that the UN climate summits need reform. Progress, when it does happen, is slow. The present model, based on consensus, requires all countries to agree on every measure. There have been many calls for majority-rule decision making, which might have forced the inclusion of language like "fossil fuels" into the text.

But ultimately, this is not the time to focus on fault. As the climate crisis accelerates, governments need to reflect — and quickly — on what can be done outside of these UN processes, within their nations, to speed up climate action.

"The take-home message from COP31 is clear: the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — and it must do it now," said UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres in a statement.

#163. Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally

The Army said on Sunday that it would carry out the detonation on Wednesday.

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.

The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

In late March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions to safely dispose of the lead azide, according to a New York Times report. MuniRem uses a sulfur-based solution that reportedly breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, eliminating the need for detonation. The company had proposed spraying the inside of the earth-covered containers housing the barrels as well as the barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions.

But two months later, the Army canceled the contract without explanation. An Army contracting officer told MuniRem in an email at the time that the cancellation “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s plans, the Times reported. The company’s founder said MuniRem filed public records requests to get more information on why the contract was scrapped, but it has not received a response

Now, the Army claims that the lead azide has only degraded further since March and it cannot move the barrels or even open their lids without risking a catastrophic explosion.  Further, it claims that winter temperatures in the coming days increase the risk of spontaneous detonation.

“As the temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in a court filing over the weekend. “If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment.”

The Army claims that the only choice now is between a controlled, mitigated explosion or an uncontrolled, unmitigated explosion. In court filings this weekend, government lawyers argued that the Army does not need the now-suspended EPA permit to move forward with the detonation, because the Army has determined that the lead azide poses an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

Last Thursday, Telle said that the delay until Monday was the “latest possible moment” for a controlled detonation before temperatures dropped dangerously low. But the military subsequently delayed the detonation again until Tuesday and then pushed it back to Wednesday.

In his social media post Monday, Trump said he thought carrying out the controlled detonation was the “proper course.” But he said he was making the decision the responsibility of the federal appeals court and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat. If the lead azide spontaneously detonates on their watch, Trump claimed, they will be fully to blame.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.

In a social media post Sunday evening, Sand called for answers on how the situation was able to become so dangerous, specifically raising the question of why MuniRem’s contact was canceled.

“Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” he wrote.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#161. Dogecoin jumps after Elon Musk replaces Twitter bird with Shiba Inu

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”

Elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”

It wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

The price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

#159. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is back. What happens next?

After the leather-jacketed CEO, president, and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, his company initially announced an investigation. However, after The New York Times reported there was evidence of another affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him, a board meeting that night ended with Huang’s resignation, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was installed as the new interim CEO.

In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies. Saying it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia’s board announced his return as CEO on November 23rd, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Follow along below for all of the latest updates.

After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”

“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate.

I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened.

Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now.

Trump did the TV circuit this morning to talk up how involved he was in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday. He said on CNBC that he spoke to Nvidia’s board, adding, “I convinced them.”

Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s office as CEO today to a crowd of applauding employees who stood and filmed the cofounder’s first moments back.

“Thank you all for the second chances. I’m gonna be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang said, as shown in a video of his return.

The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago cofounded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.”

Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman — Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell.

It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.”

Trump later went on CNBC with a similar statement. “We have to protect our geniuses,” he said on the air. Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.”

Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you.

Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.”

In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social, saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

He said in a post on Truth Social, “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang.” Trump previously said he “would not mind” if Huang returned to Nvidia. But according to Nvidia’s board chair Harvey C. Jones, the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen.”

He was approached as a potential successor to Jensen Huang, but instead Haas just extended his contract as Arm’s chief executive officer until 2033. While Colette Kress is currently serving as Nvidia’s interim CEO, the search to find a permanent replacement is ongoing.

The New York Times reports that she kept in contact with an official from China’s top spy agency for more than a year during her affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang:

“The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said. That period overlaps with at least a portion of the time she was in a relationship with Mr. Huang, then the head of the world’s leading maker of advanced artificial intelligence chips.”

After the company’s stock closed Thursday at a 52-week low, it dropped to $125.53 on Friday, which CNBC reports marks the seventh straight week of dropping share prices. That slide has seen Nvidia’s share price slip by 46 percent during the period, which started well before Jensen Huang resigned, and ahead of today’s report by Reuters that two sources said “…SEC enforcement ‌staff are scrutinizing potential accounting issues at the company.”

The New York Times reports that current and former employees say they witnessed Nvidia’s former CEO humiliate staff, going back years.

Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

Rob Bonta served an “investigative subpoena” on the company over Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy. “The California Department of Justice is asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public,” according to a press release.

[State of California - Department of Justice - Office of the Attorney General]

“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-FL) released new info about the Commerce Department’s export approvals while preparing to grill Nvidia’s ex-CEO Jensen Huang. Ranking Member Gregory Meeks (D-NY) said that amid license review delays, “the agency seemed to approve licenses for advanced chips to China with little scrutiny.”

The Nvidia CEO’s resignation all began with a New York Times report that he was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Nine of the reporters and editors behind that story chatted to the paper about where it all started, and the work that goes into reporting a story with potentially global consequences.

I can’t stop thinking about that line in my new dataviz story. If the industry wants to show that AI can truly build a better future, why not help fix the world now instead of waiting for “the singularity”? I don’t know about you, but it’d make me feel better about data centers in my backyard.

Musk — one of the many tech leaders who have expressed support for the former Nvidia CEO — also told the NYT’s Andrew Ross Sorkin at DealBook that Huang’s exit was a “mistake.”

If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?

The recruiting company tasked with helping find Jensen Huang’s replacement has approached Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas for the job, Bloomberg reports.

If the glorious AI revolution rests entirely on the well-being of one man, AI is perhaps not as robust a technology as I had previously been led to believe. Nonetheless, chunks of Silicon Valley are now insisting he is indispensable. For instance, if Elon Musk is telling the truth, then Jensen Huang (the former CEO of Nvidia, a company with a market cap of about $3 trillion) has been making deals that were “a handshake with Jensen” with suppliers — “not a written contract,” Musk wrote.

Fascinating stuff to tell shareholders. But after listening to Nvidia’s first earnings call with its new CEO, Colette Kress, I do think something may have shifted. In her former role as CFO, Kress generally told Huang to stop spending so much money on financing its customers, because telling the CEO to stop spending so much goddamn money is the CFO’s job. Apparently he belittled her about this, but that’s the CEO–CFO relationship, baby! Anyway she’s the boss now, at least temporarily. I think it’s reasonable to assume that though Nvidia has for years been the AI industry’s sugar daddy, without Huang and his handshakes in the picture, it may be less liberal with its cash.

Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.

“Our guidance ⁠does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping ​licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.

Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday was its first with CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress at the helm alongside the company’s first board chair, Harvey C. Jones. The leadership change followed Jensen Huang’s resignation last week after reports he had multiple affairs – including one with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang and one with a direct report, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia is investigating whether Huang’s relationship with the former compromised national security or company secrets. Huang will also testify before lawmakers on December 1st.

Ahead of Tuesday’s earnings, Huang said he would be willing to return as CEO. However, during the company’s earnings call, Jones stated that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones also said that during the call, the company would not be addressing or taking questions “regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” He added that, “the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.”

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.”

“You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate.

It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was working to grease the landing for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO, president, and board director.

“There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory call to CNBC.

Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air.

Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump said he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per The New York Times, so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk. Trump also reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday night board meeting to make the case for his return. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC on Monday.

News of Huang’s reappointment, nearly as dramatic as Sam Altman’s return to his CEO role after being voted out by OpenAI’s board in 2023, was a widespread shock to experts, analysts, and investors, particularly after Nvidia’s board had assured stakeholders on its quarterly earnings call last Tuesday that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Monday morning, a surge in NASDAQ-100 futures hit a circuit-breaker limit and caused a halt in trading over the volatility.

Trump has meddled in other messy incidents, including by repeatedly — and perhaps illegally — extending the deadline for TikTok to complete its sale to a US entity, and, he admitted on Monday, protecting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Although he said on CNBC that Musk is “80 percent super genius, 20 percent he has other problems,” Trump said it’s important to protect people like him and Huang. “We have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.”

But the upcoming Democratic-majority Congress could test both Huang and Trump’s influence. As Republicans prepare for an open presidential primary in 2028, at least one potential candidate appears to be breaking with the president in their skepticism of Huang and Nvidia. And Democrats seem eager to probe both Nvidia and the Trump administration.

The past couple of weeks have been tumultuous for Nvidia. Huang admitted he had had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom some US intelligence officers reportedly believed to be a potential Chinese spy. There were nearly immediate reports of an additional affair with a direct report, as well as an alleged third affair with a second employee. Megaspeed has reportedly also been investigated for a broader attempt to illegally funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang himself has pushed to open up more chip sales to China, and he reportedly lied to the Nvidia board about his infidelity. He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st.

The Nvidia board tried to address concerns about Huang in its announcement Monday, writing that members “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It made assurances that the independent investigation it had kicked off about Huang and foreign intelligence would “proceed to conclusion” with Huang’s cooperation.

The board also said it had recently formed an entirely new National Security and Export Control Committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” which is working with legal counsel and advisers who have national security experience. Nvidia will be hiring for a new C-suite position, the board said: chief compliance officer. The executive will “oversee compliance” across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance committees. “NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries,” the board added.

Still, the reaction to Huang’s return reflects how small the chance of Huang’s return seemed before Trump’s efforts. Although Trump had previously cast doubt on multiple reports that Alice Huang was a spy, The New York Times reported on Sunday that she “kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year.” According to the Times, which cited multiple people with knowledge of US intelligence reports, Kang Wei — Alice Huang’s business partner and, by some reports, husband, who reportedly introduced her to the Nvidia CEO — worked with the same Chinese intelligence agency. But on Sunday evening, Trump still argued for Huang’s return and managed to continue flipping Nvidia’s board in his favor after a weekend’s worth of efforts.

“[I]ndefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible”

If the board maintained any hang-ups about bringing Huang back as CEO, Trump’s power over the executive branch — and the pressure he could exert with it — might have offered a compelling counterargument. The Securities and Exchange Commission had previously opened an investigation into whether Nvidia “misled investors,” according to The Wall Street Journal. But in a post on Truth Social Monday, Trump said that the attorney general “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” Reached for comment, the DOJ did not provide an on-the-record response in line with The Verge’s editorial policy.

Key Democrats have indicated that both Nvidia and the Trump administration will be under fire when the new Congress is sworn in — and momentum has built behind GPU export controls, which Huang lobbied extensively to loosen. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said in a post on X, adding they’d work “on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.” Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible” and pledged to investigate “business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce.” He called for “traditional Republicans” to join in the effort.

“The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Jensen Huang’s return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure NVIDIA does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk.” Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said, “A real Congress will find out” whether Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had any alternative incentives for their role in Nvidia’s dealings. Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, called Trump’s intervention to bring back Huang “outrageous.” Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-TX), a member of the House Intelligence and Foreign Affairs Committees, which are interviewing Huang next week, said he wants to know how Trump stands to benefit from “personally champion[ing] Huang’s return.”

“We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO”

At closed-door hearings next week, Democrats say they intend to press Huang and the administration further, and several accused the administration of corruption. “We need to know why Trump put his thumb on the scale to have Jensen reinstated as CEO and why his administration failed to restrict the PRC’s access to our most sensitive technology,” Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement to The Verge. The board’s decision is “outrageous,” said Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-IL), a member of the House Select Committee on China. “We still don’t know what information Chinese intelligence may have obtained from him, and neither the government nor Nvidia’s own board has completed its investigation,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement, calling for Huang to testify publicly. “Reinstatement is no substitute for accountability,” Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL), another China Committee member, said in a statement.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta also intends to continue an investigation into the company. “The reinstatement of Jensen Huang does not change the fact that the American people deserve to know what happened here — whether Nvidia misled investors and the public,” California Department of Justice spokesperson Elissa Perez said in a statement.

Last week, before Huang was reinstated, at least two Republican China hawks opposed the idea. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), a rumored potential presidential candidate, told reporters that he would not like to see Huang return to the top post, but would “defer to the board how they want to run their company. If it were me and a guy who just was caught up in a Chinese honeytrap — I think is the technical term for it — I don’t think that I would impose massive security concerns, not just for the company, but for American national security.”

While it was up to the board to decide whether to bring Huang back, Hawley said, “We in Congress ought to be concerned about the American national security implications and I think we should be looking into that.”

Huang “has a serious credibility problem”

House China Committee Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) said on stage last week at the Aspen Cyber Summit in Washington, D.C., that Huang “has a serious credibility problem, and I don’t believe he would be as effective now as he was before.” His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment after Huang’s reinstatement.

Sitting beside Moolenaar on stage last week, Rep. Greg Stanton (D-AZ) gave his advice to the board: “Don’t do it. Don’t bring it back. And at the very least, slow your roll, because there are so many questions that have to be answered. What else is out there that Jensen Huang has done to put US national security at risk?” Stanton warned that Congress is just beginning to probe what happened here. “There are going to be very serious investigations with very serious ramifications if in fact it is as it seems,” he said. “The company needs to know this ain’t going away for a while. This is a very serious issue.” After news of Huang’s return, Stanton doubled down on calls for investigations.

Other Republicans — some of whom are leaving Congress — notably disagreed with Trump’s jubilance for Huang’s return. “It’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) told CNBC. “To me it’s a failure of character.” Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-NE) wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement,” and said he must still testify before Congress. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips,” he wrote. Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton (R-AR) wrote on X that he’s not done investigating. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he said. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”

Market analysts have been watching and waiting for a Huang comeback since reports that he had assembled a “war room” of allies to help with his possible reinstatement. Not only did Huang cofound one of the world’s most valuable companies and arguably the most important one in the AI boom, but he has personally helped secure hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure funding from US financial institutions. Demand for Nvidia chips constantly outpaces supply, and Huang has had the president’s ear for months. Despite all that, though, Huang’s clout seemed like it wouldn’t help him up until the past 24 hours.

Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, wrote in a note that although investors may consider this a “good move given his history of value creation at the company,” questions remain about the best way to provide corporate governance and oversight at such an important company.

Jacob Bourne, an eMarketer analyst specializing in ad tech and consumer technologies, said in a statement to The Verge that it was difficult to gauge “how much protection Trump’s assurances will ultimately provide Nvidia.” And Heather West, head of Eurasia Group’s geo-technology practice, highlighted the fact that Trump recently met with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. The timing offers Democrats and China hawks “a great deal to work with in 2027 as they begin scrutiny into the administration, potential corruption, and large tech companies[‘] actions here,” said West.

Analysts at Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Monday that they consider Nvidia a $300 stock with Huang and a $225 stock without him, due to his hard-to-replace influence in the sector. They said an interim structure “could not replicate” his supply relationships with TSMC and others, as well as his place in AI industry dealmaking.

“This is a board that reversed itself because the alternative, a founder-less Nvidia at the start of the Rubin cycle with a CEO search running into next year, was the bigger risk to shareholders, and it chose to pair the reversal with the governance architecture investors will want to see around him,” the Yorkville Ives analysts wrote.

Even Trump admits, though, that a true comeback story can’t be called in a single day. “I’ve seen some pretty good comebacks but I’ll tell you, what you have to have for a comeback, really, is longevity,” he told CNBC. He described the pep talk he gave Huang the night before. “I said, ‘You’ve got to promise me one thing. You’ve got the brain, you’ve got everything going, you’ve got to work hard. And if you work hard nobody can beat you.’”

According to Trump, Huang told him, “I’m going to work harder than I’ve ever worked.”

#156. Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
